# A linear, second-order, unconditionally energy-stable scalar-auxiliary-variable scheme for the CHQ viscoelastic phase-separation model

**Abstract**

The CHQ model describes viscoelastic phase separation in a polymer–solvent mixture: a Cahn–Hilliard equation for the polymer volume fraction \(\phi\) is two-way coupled, through a phase-dependent cross-diffusion flux, to a damped relaxation equation for a scalar bulk elastic stress _q_. We propose a scalar-auxiliary-variable (SAV) time discretisation of this system, combining the SAV reformulation of the double-well potential with a second-order backward differentiation formula (BDF2) and a second-order extrapolation of all phase-dependent mobilities: a linear, computationally cheaper complement to the reference scheme’s fully nonlinear Newton solve. The resulting method is (i) linear at every time step, with a coupling structure we prove has exactly one solution at every step, for every choice of time-step size; (ii) mass conserving, exactly, as an algebraic identity of the discrete equations themselves (the only drift ever seen numerically traces to the finite tolerance of the iterative linear solver, not a failure of the conservation property); and (iii) unconditionally stable for a modified discrete energy, via an exact one-step energy–dissipation identity. We show the energy identity extends to this filtered variant as well, with two explicit extra non-negative terms. Hence, the scheme actually producing the physics results is itself provably stable for the same energy. A Fourier–Galerkin implementation verifies that the energy identity holds at every time step to within floating-point round-off. It also confirms second-order temporal accuracy, including in the steep-interface regime, and agreement with an independently implemented nonlinear Newton–BDF2 solver. Compared with that independent nonlinear Newton–BDF2 solver, at equal grid resolution, the SAV method uses 2.5–3.0\(\times\) fewer linear-solver iterations and 1.7–2.0\(\times\) less wall-clock time.

### 1 Introduction

#### 1.1 The model

Phase separation in polymer solutions and melts is frequently accompanied by a pronounced viscoelastic response: the slower-relaxing polymer network resists deformation on the timescale of demixing, and the resulting elastic stress can dramatically alter, and in some cases arrest, the coarsening process compared to a simple binary fluid. The same coupling between phase separation and viscoelasticity is central to biomolecular condensates in living cells [1]. Condensates themselves age into viscoelastic, Maxwell-fluid-like materials rather than remaining simple liquids [2], and the surrounding chromatin network has been shown experimentally to slow the coalescence of nucleolar droplets by orders of magnitude relative to isolated liquid droplets, an arrest effect closely analogous to the elastic suppression of coarsening studied here [3]. More directly still, recent experiments show that tuning the viscoelastic properties of a nucleus-mimicking compartment controls the dynamics and liquid-to-solid transition of protein condensates [4]. This phenomenon, reviewed by Tanaka [5] and modelled by a hierarchy of increasingly reduced continuum descriptions,

couples a Cahn-Hilliard-type phase-field equation to an evolution equation for the elastic stress through a cross-diffusion flux. This structure is numerically delicate: energy-stable schemes for the uncoupled Cahn-Hilliard equation do not automatically extend to the coupled system, and the reference discretisation for exactly this reduced model \[6\] requires a nonlinear solve at every time step. This paper shows that a linear scheme can retain the same unconditional energy stability.

The scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) approach \[7, 8\] is a general strategy for exactly this kind of question: introducing one extra scalar unknown that tracks the square root of the (shifted) nonlinear part of the energy turns the troublesome nonlinear term (the derivative \(f'(\phi)\) of the double-well potential in (1b) below) into a linear one, at the cost of solving one additional, cheap scalar equation each step. Applied to a single Cahn-Hilliard equation this already gives a linear, unconditionally energy-stable scheme with no step-size restriction and no extra stabilisation term added by hand, the usual efficiency case made for SAV schemes. It is, however, nontrivial to extend this to the viscoelastic phase separation model given by Equation 1 below, where the SAV-linearised equation for the density \(\phi\) and the equation for the stress _q_ are coupled through the same cross-diffusion flux (Section 1.4).

Following Spiller et al. \[9\], Zhou et al. \[10\], and Brunk et al. \[6\], we consider a model without hydrodynamics that has the polymer volume fraction \(\phi\), the chemical potential \(\mu\), and a single scalar bulk elastic variable _q_ as dynamical variables. We consider the following system on a periodic domain \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) for \(t\in(0,T)\):

\(\partial_t\phi=\nabla\cdot(b(\phi)\nabla\mu-c(\phi)\nabla(A(\phi)q))\big),\) (1a)

\(\mu=-\gamma\Delta\phi+f'(\phi),\) (1b)

\(\partial_tq=-\kappa(\phi)q-A(\phi)\nabla\cdot\big(c(\phi)\nabla\mu-d_0\nabla(A(\phi)q)\big)+\varepsilon_q\Delta q,\) (1c)

The analysis below is independent of the spatial dimension _d_, although our numerical experiments use _d_=2. We impose periodic boundary conditions to eliminate boundary terms in the integration-by-parts identities used in Section 3.1 and to match the Fourier spectral discretisation described in Section 6. At the continuous level, other boundary conditions that eliminate the same boundary terms, such as suitable no-flux conditions, would also suffice. Here, \(\gamma>0\) is the gradient-energy coefficient, \(d_0,\varepsilon_q>0\) are constants, and _f_ is a double-well potential bounded from below. The functions \(b,c,A,\kappa\) depend on the phase field \(\phi\) and satisfy \(b,\kappa>0\) and \(c,A\ge 0\).

## 1.2 Energy structure

Equations (1) describe a system relaxing towards thermodynamic equilibrium: \(\phi\) and _q_ evolve so as to decrease a single scalar quantity _E_, with the terms on the right of (1) acting as dissipative (frictional) driving forces whose strength is set by the state-dependent coefficients \(b(\phi),c(\phi),A(\phi)\), together with, for _q_, additional linear damping from the \(-\kappa(\phi)q\) and \(\varepsilon_q\Delta q\) terms in (1c). We define the energy as

\(E(\phi,q)=\int_\Omega\big[\frac{\gamma}{2}|\nabla\phi|^2+f(\phi)+\frac{1}{2}q^2\big]\mathrm{d}x,\) (2)

a sum of three physically distinct contributions: the interfacial energy \(\frac{\gamma}{2}|\nabla\phi|^2\), which penalises sharp changes in composition and so favours smooth, spread-out interfaces; the bulk free energy \(f(\phi)\), a double-well potential favouring the two pure phases \(\phi\approx 0,1\) and so driving phase separation; and the elastic energy \(\frac{1}{2}q^2\) stored in the polymer network, penalising deviations of the elastic variable _q_ away from its relaxed value _q_=0.

For sufficiently smooth solutions that are periodic in space, the energy satisfies a dissipation law, (<tbc>

<tbc>d<tbc>

<tbc>_E_=-D), as shown in Section 2. The dissipation rate is non-negative only under a suitable condition on the model coefficients. We derive this condition, called the coercivity condition, and establish the continuous energy law in Section 2.

## 1.3 Related work

Brunk, Egger, Habrich and Lukácová-Medvidová \[6\] (Correction \[11\]) give a rigorously analysed, fully nonlinear finite-element / variational-in-time discretisation of (1) with an exact energy identity and order-optimal error estimates via relative energy, and name the SAV route as future work for cheaper solves. Strasser, Tierra, Dünweg and Lukácová-Medvidová \[12, 13\] give linear, energy-stable schemes for the full hydrodynamic polymer–solvent model by a secant linearisation (not SAV), without an error analysis. Structural cousins include a Cahn–Hilliard/Allen–Cahn cross-kinetic coupling \[14\], viscoelastic Cahn–Hilliard models discretised by compactness-driven (not SAV, not linear) schemes \[15, 16\], and the nearest SAV scheme for any mechanically-coupled phase-field model, a Caginalp/elastic-solid system \[17\] structurally distinct from (1). The SAV approach itself \[7, 8, 18\] and the frozen-mobility-at-extrapolated-state device \[19\] are established for scalar gradient flows; single-auxiliary-variable SAV has been used for other coupled Cahn– Hilliard systems \[20, 21\]. To the best of our knowledge, no SAV, IEQ, or energy-quadratisation discretisation has previously been proposed for (1), or for any viscoelastic Cahn–Hilliard model with this cross-diffusion structure.

## 1.4 Contribution

For standard Cahn–Hilliard-type gradient flows, the SAV device separates the nonlinear free- energy term from the remaining linear operator by freezing it at an extrapolated state, and the resulting scheme’s energy stability then follows term by term. In (1), however, \(\phi\) and _q_ are coupled through the same phase-dependent cross-diffusion flux \(c(\phi)\nabla(A(\phi)q)\), entering the two equations with opposite sign: freezing _c_ and _A_ independently, or at the new-time solution, breaks the exact coupled-dissipation structure that produces the dissipation term (3) in the continuous energy law, and reintroduces a \(\Delta t\)-dependent remainder that would have to be absorbed by a stabilisation term or a step-size restriction. The observation underlying Theorem 4.1 below is that freezing all of \(b,c,A,\kappa\) at one common extrapolated state \(\phi^\star\) preserves this cross-diffusion structure exactly, so the SAV reformulation and the BDF2 energy identity combine with no such remainder and no restriction on \(\Delta t\).

The new contribution of this work is not the SAV device or the extrapolation device in isolation, but to show that they together survive the _coupled_ cross-diffusion dissipation structure of (1). Concretely:

(i) an SAV–BDF2 discretisation of the full coupled system, linear at every step, with a proof (Theorem 4.1) that the modified-energy identity (12) extends exactly to the coupled dissipation form with the \(A(\phi)\)-weighted test (holding for any time step \(\Delta t>0\), with no stabilisation term and no \(\|\phi^{n+1}-\phi^\star\|\) remainder), together with an extension (Remark 4.2) to the post-step spectral-filtering variant actually used for the physics study;<tbc>

(ii) a per-step solvability theorem (Theorem 5.1): the linear system (S1)–(S4) is uniquely solvable for every \(\Delta t>0\);<tbc>

(iii) numerical verification: the identity to round-off, second-order temporal accuracy at the physical \(\gamma=10^{-3}\), spectral spatial accuracy on the smooth test problems considered, agreement with an independent nonlinear solver, and a clean cost comparison.

The present work is complementary to that of Ref. \[6\], not an improvement on its analysis; we do not claim a rigorous error estimate.

### Outline.

Section 2 derives the continuous energy law and its SAV reformulation. Section 3 states the discrete scheme. Section 4 proves the discrete energy identity, the paper’s main result. Section 5 establishes solvability and mass conservation. Section 6 discusses accuracy and the Fourier–Galerkin implementation. Section 7 collects the numerical evidence: the identity to<tbc>

round-off, convergence, agreement with independent solvers, cost, and the coupled-vs-uncoupled demonstration. Proofs are given as concise sketches in the main text; fuller derivations are collected in Appendix A.

## 2 The continuous energy law and its SAV reformulation

We first establish the energy-decay property of the continuous model (1), introduced in Section 1.2. We show not only that the energy _E_ decreases over time, but also derive an explicit decay rate in terms of the model’s coefficients. The numerical scheme in Section 3 will be designed to reproduce this decay rate exactly at the discrete level.

**Proposition 2.1.** _Let_ \((\phi,\mu,q)\) _solve_ (1)_. Then_ \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}E=-\mathcal{D}\) _with_

\(\mathcal{D}=\int_\Omega\big[\big(b(\phi)-\frac{c(\phi)^2}{d_0}\big)|\nabla\mu|^2+\frac{1}{d_0}\big|c(\phi)\nabla\mu-d_0\nabla(A(\phi)q)\big|^2+\kappa(\phi)q^2+\varepsilon_q|\nabla q|^2\big]\mathrm{d}x,\) (3)

_and_ \(\mathcal{D}\ge 0\) _whenever_ \(b(\phi)d_0\ge c(\phi)^2\) _pointwise, the coercivity condition_ (5).

_Proof._ Differentiating _E_, substituting (1b), and integrating by parts gives \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}E=\big(\mu,\partial_t\phi\big)+\big(q,\partial_tq\big)\). Pairing (1a) with \(\mu\) and (1c) with _q_ (that is, multiplying each equation by the stated function and integrating over \(\Omega\)), the two resulting cross terms are equal rather than cancelling, by the sign convention adopted in (1a). The elementary identity

\(b|u|^2-2c\left(u\cdot w\right)+d_0|w|^2=\big(b-\frac{c^2}{d_0}\big)|u|^2+\frac{1}{d_0}\big|cu-d_0w\big|^2\) (4)

applied pointwise with \(u=\nabla\mu\), \(w=\nabla(Aq)\) then gives (3). This continuous dissipation identity is already implicit in \[6, 9\]. We record it here, with the sign convention and coercivity threshold made explicit, as the baseline the discrete scheme of Section 3 is required to reproduce. Full proof in Appendix A.

The energy _E_ satisfies \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}E=-\mathcal{D}\) but nothing guarantees \(\mathcal{D}\ge 0\) for an arbitrary choice of the coefficients \(b,c,A,\kappa\). Checking this directly is exactly what produces the one structural condition the coefficients must satisfy. The first two terms in the dissipation rate (3) form a quadratic expression in \(\nabla\mu\) and \(\nabla(A(\phi)q)\). By (4), this expression is non-negative for arbitrary values of these gradients if and only if

\(b(\phi)d_0\ge c(\phi)^2\text{for all admissible}\phi.\) (5)

The remaining terms in (3) are non-negative because \(\kappa(\phi)>0\) and \(\varepsilon_q>0\). Thus, the coercivity condition (5) guarantees that the continuous energy is non-increasing. This condition is Assumption (A1) of \[6\].

### 2.1 The SAV reformulation

Proposition 2.1 establishes the continuous energy law. We now focus on discretising (1). The only nonlinear term is \(f'(\phi)\) in the \(\mu\)-equation (1b), which comes from the double-well potential _f_. The scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) method removes this nonlinearity by introducing a scalar unknown _r(t_), a single real number at each time, rather than a new field over \(\Omega\). The resulting enlarged system has exactly the same solutions as the original system, but no longer contains \(f'(\phi)\) explicitly.

The construction starts by separating the part of the energy that is already at most quadratic from the part that carries the nonlinearity. Specifically, we write _E=E_<sub>lin</sub>+_E<sub>f</sub>_ with<tbc>

\(E_\mathrm{lin}:=\int_\Omega\big[\frac{\gamma}{2}|\nabla\phi|^2+\frac{1}{2}q^2\big]\mathrm{d}x,E_f:=\int_\Omega f(\phi)\mathrm{d}x.\)

<tbc>Since _f_ is bounded below, we may fix a constant _C_<sub>0</sub> large enough that \(E_f(\phi)+C_0\ge C_1>0\) for every admissible \(\phi\) (any _C_<sub>0</sub>_\>_0 works for our benchmark, where \(f\ge 0\) already; we use _C_<sub>0</sub>=1); this positivity is needed so that the square root<tbc>

\(r(t):=\sqrt{E_f(\phi(t))+C_0},G(\phi):=\frac{f'(\phi)}{\sqrt{E_f(\phi)+C_0}}\)

<tbc>is always well defined. Here _r(t_) is a single scalar that tracks, at every instant, the size of the nonlinear part of the energy along the solution, and _G_ is a new coefficient function chosen for exactly one reason: by construction, \(rG(\phi)=f'(\phi)\) whenever _r_ happens to take the value \(\sqrt{E_f(\phi)+C_0}\). This suggests replacing the troublesome \(f'(\phi)\) in (1b) by the product \(rG(\phi)\) and treating _r_ as an independent unknown, governed by its own evolution equation,

\(\dot{r}=\frac{1}{2}\big(G(\phi),\partial_t\phi\big),\)

appended to the system. The evolution equation for _r_ follows directly from differentiating \(r=\sqrt{E_f(\phi)+C_0}\) using the chain rule (Appendix A). Consequently, if this relation holds initially, it is preserved throughout the evolution. Introducing _r_ also allows \(G(\phi)\) to be treated as a coefficient function, alongside _b,c,A_, and \(\kappa\). In the discrete scheme of Section 3, these coefficients are evaluated at the extrapolated state. This reformulation makes the \(\mu\)-equation linear in the joint unknowns \((\phi,\mu,q,r)\), regardless of the form of the double-well potential _f_.

This substitution is legitimate because the enlarged system has exactly the same solutions as the original (1). We show in Appendix A that the appended equation for _r_ forces \(r(t)\equiv\sqrt{E_f(\phi(t))+C_0}\) along every solution, given matching initial data, so that \(r(t)G(\phi(t))\equiv f'(\phi(t))\) identically and the SAV \(\mu\)-equation reduces back to (1b). Along any such solution the modified energy

\(\widetilde{E}:=E_\mathrm{lin}+r^2-C_0\)

is therefore identically equal to the true energy _E_, and satisfies a dissipation law of exactly the same completed-square form as before, \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\widetilde{E}=-\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}\le 0\), with \(\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}\) built from (3) in the same way, only with \(f'(\phi)\) replaced by \(rG(\phi)\) throughout. Note that _q_’s contribution to the energy, \(\frac{1}{2}q^2\), is already quadratic, so it needs no auxiliary variable of its own; only the single genuinely nonlinear piece _f_ is quadratised, and a single extra scalar _r_ suffices for the whole system, regardless of how finely \(\Omega\) is resolved.

One caveat carries forward to the numerical scheme and is worth flagging now. The identity \(r(t)\equiv\sqrt{E_f(\phi(t))+C_0}\) above holds exactly only because, in continuous time, two quantities that start out equal and change at the same rate at every instant must stay equal forever. Once time is replaced by discrete steps (Section 3), _r_<sup>_n_+1</sup> is no longer obtained from that continuous argument: it is computed by advancing a difference equation one step at a time, and nothing forces this step-by-step update to reproduce \(\sqrt{E_f(\phi^{n+1})+C_0}\) exactly. The two quantities, _r<sup>n</sup>_ and \(\sqrt{E_f(\phi^n)+C_0}\), can therefore differ by a small, controlled amount. This is exactly where the modified and true discrete energies can differ (Remark 4.3 discusses this in detail).

## 3 The SAV-BDF2 scheme

Section 2 established that the continuous, SAV-reformulated system dissipates its modified energy exactly, with no restriction on the coefficients beyond coercivity. Turning this into a usable numerical method needs two further ingredients: a way to approximate the time derivatives \(\partial_t\phi,\partial_tq,\dot{r}\) to second order in the step size \(\Delta t\), and a way to evaluate the phase-dependent coefficients \(b,c,A,\kappa,G\) without reintroducing the very nonlinearity the SAV device was meant to remove. The first is supplied by a standard second-order finite-difference formula in time, BDF2. The second is this paper’s central device, already previewed in Section 1.4: evaluate every coefficient not at the unknown new state \(\phi^{n+1}\), but at an already-known approximation to<tbc>

it, extrapolated from the two previous time levels. This section makes both ingredients precise and states the resulting scheme. Then in Section 4, we show that combining them preserves the energy identity exactly.

## 3.1 Notation

We define the scalar product as \(\big(u,v\big):=\int_\Omega uv\mathrm{d}x\) and the norm as \(\|u\|^2:=\big(u,u\big)\). On the periodic box, with no boundary terms, we have

\(\big(\nabla\cdot F,g\big)=-\big(F,\nabla g\big),\) (6a)

\(\big(\Delta u,g\big)=-\big(\nabla u,\nabla g\big).\) (6b)

The second identity follows from the first by taking \(F=\nabla u\).

Time derivatives are approximated by BDF2, the second-order backward differentiation formula: a standard finite-difference rule that approximates \(\dot{u}(t_{n+1})\) using the current level together with the two preceding ones, _u_<sup>_n_+1</sup>_,u<sup>n</sup>,u_<sup>_n_-1</sup> (as opposed to the simpler, only first-order- accurate backward-Euler rule, which uses just _u_<sup>_n_+1</sup>_,u<sup>n</sup>_). Write \(t_n=n\Delta t\) for the time levels and _u<sup>n</sup>≈u(t<sub>n</sub>_) for a numerical approximation at level _n_; a superscript ⋆ will denote a quantity frozen at the extrapolated state \(\phi^\star\), introduced below. Specifically, we define the BDF2 first and second time differences

\(D_2u^{n+1}:=\frac{3u^{n+1}-4u^n+u^{n-1}}{2\Delta t},D^2u^{n+1}:=u^{n+1}-2u^n+u^{n-1}.\) (7)

_D_<sub>2</sub>_u_<sup>_n_+1</sup> is the actual BDF2 approximation to \(\dot{u}(t_{n+1})\), accurate to \(O(\Delta t^2)\); _D_<sup>2</sup>_u_<sup>_n_+1</sup> is not itself an approximation to anything, but a bookkeeping quantity that will appear naturally, in Section 4, as the non-negative remainder left over after telescoping a BDF2 term into a discrete energy difference.

## 3.2 Freezing the coefficients

The one remaining obstacle to a linear scheme is that \(b,c,A,\kappa\) (and, after Section 2’s reformulation, _G_) are themselves functions of \(\phi\). Evaluating them at the unknown \(\phi^{n+1}\) being solved for would make every equation below nonlinear in \(\phi^{n+1}\), exactly the nonlinearity a Newton-type solver would have to iterate on instead; evaluating them at an already known approximation to \(\phi(t_{n+1})\) keeps every equation linear in the actual unknowns, at the cost of a small, controllable extrapolation error. Since \(\phi^n,\phi^{n-1}\) are already known once we reach time level _n_+1, we define the extrapolation<tbc>

\(\phi^\star:=2\phi^n-\phi^{n-1},\)

<tbc>a new value recomputed at every step from the two preceding ones. So, \(\phi^\star\) depends on _n_ exactly as \(\phi^n\) does, but we write \(\phi^\star\) rather than \(\phi^{\star,n+1}\) purely to keep the notation light. \(\phi^\star\) approximates \(\phi(t_{n+1})\) to \(O(\Delta t^2)\), of the same order as that achieved by BDF2. However, using \(\phi^\star=\phi^n\) instead would only be accurate to \(O(\Delta t)\) and would degrade the scheme’s overall accuracy. For the specific coefficient forms of the benchmark problem (\[6\], given in full in Section 7), \(A(\phi)\sim\mathrm{cot}(\pi\phi)\) and \(\kappa(\phi)\) blow up as \(\phi\rightarrow 0,1\); to guard against \(\phi^\star\) straying outside the physically admissible range before the scheme has had a chance to correct it, we additionally clamp it to the interval \([\delta_c,1-\delta_c]\),<tbc>

\(\phi_b^\star:=\mathrm{clamp}(\phi^\star,\delta_c,1-\delta_c):=\mathrm{min}\big(\mathrm{max}(\phi^\star,\delta_c),1-\delta_c\big),\delta_c\sim 10^{-3}\)

<tbc>(a numerical safeguard only, verified inactive throughout the convergence regime studied below). Every phase-dependent coefficient is then frozen at this same argument,<tbc>

\(b_\star:=b(\phi_b^\star),c_\star:=c(\phi_b^\star),A_\star:=A(\phi_b^\star),\kappa_\star:=\kappa(\phi_b^\star),G_\star:=\frac{f'(\phi^\star)}{\sqrt{E_f(\phi^\star)+C_0}},\) (8)

using the same clamped state for all four of \(b,c,A,\kappa\), for uniformity, although strictly the clamp only matters for \(A,\kappa\), whose specific forms would otherwise be singular. The parameters _b,c_ remain well behaved throughout the range for the coefficient forms used here and _G<sub>⋆</sub>_ uses the unclamped \(\phi^\star\) throughout, since \(f'\) and _E<sub>f</sub>_ do not develop singularities either. This is the step, previewed in Section 1.4, on which the rest of the paper turns: freezing all of \(b,c,A,\kappa\) at the same state, rather than at several different ones or at \(\phi^{n+1}\) itself, is exactly what preserves the coupled cross-diffusion structure of (1) intact, as Section 4 shows next.

**Assumption 1** (Frozen coercivity)**.** We assume that \(b_\star(x)-c_\star(x)^2/d_0\ge 0\) for all _x_. This is the same coercivity condition as (5), evaluated at the frozen, clamped state \(s=\phi_b^\star(x)\). For the benchmark coefficient set, the condition is satisfied with \(b_\star-c_\star^2/d_0=\varepsilon_b\) at every point. Thus, the coercivity margin is strictly positive and independent of the time step \(\Delta t\).

### 3.3 The discrete scheme

The scheme advances only the variables \(\phi\), _q_, and _r_, since these are the three quantities governed by evolution equations in (1). Accordingly, the scheme must retain their values at the previous two time levels. The chemical potential \(\mu\), by contrast, is defined algebraically by (1b) as an instantaneous function of \(\phi\) and, following the SAV reformulation, _r_, at the current time level. Since \(\mu\) has no independent evolution equation, its value is recomputed at each time step from the current values of these variables. Consequently, neither \(\mu^n\) nor \(\mu^{n-1}\) is required by the scheme, and neither appears in the formulation below.

Collecting the pieces above, the scheme is obtained from the continuous system (1) by three simultaneous replacements: every time derivative \(\partial_t\) is replaced by the BDF2 operator _D_<sub>2</sub>, every phase-dependent coefficient is replaced by its frozen value (8), and the SAV auxiliary equation for _r_ from Section 2 is adjoined as a fourth equation. We label the resulting four equations (S1)-(S4) (“S” for “scheme”) to keep them visually distinct from the continuous model’s (1a)-(1c). For \(n\ge 1\), given \((\phi^{n-1},q^{n-1},r^{n-1})\) and \((\phi^n,q^n,r^n)\), we find \((\phi^{n+1},\mu^{n+1},q^{n+1},r^{n+1})\) solving

\(D_2\phi^{n+1}=\nabla\cdot\big(b_\star\nabla\mu^{n+1}-c_\star\nabla(A_\star q^{n+1})\big),\) (S1)

\(\mu^{n+1}=-\gamma\Delta\phi^{n+1}+r^{n+1}G_\star,\) (S2)

\(D_2q^{n+1}=-\kappa_\star q^{n+1}-A_\star\nabla\cdot\big(c_\star\nabla\mu^{n+1}-d_0\nabla(A_\star q^{n+1})\big)+\varepsilon_q\Delta q^{n+1},\) (S3)

\(D_2r^{n+1}=\frac{1}{2}\big(G_\star,D_2\phi^{n+1}\big).\) (S4)

By construction, each equation is linear in the unknowns \((\phi^{n+1},\mu^{n+1},q^{n+1},r^{n+1})\), since all coefficients are evaluated using the frozen, already-known quantities in (8), rather than the unknown \(\phi^{n+1}\) itself. The only coupling that prevents the four equations from being block- diagonal arises in (S4), where the scalar unknown _r_<sup>_n_+1</sup> is coupled to all degrees of freedom of \(\phi^{n+1}\) through the single scalar quantity \(\big(G_\star,D_2\phi^{n+1}\big)\). Section 5 exploits this specific structure to avoid solving the full coupled system simultaneously.

BDF2 itself needs two prior levels to get started, so the very first step, from \((\phi^0,q^0,r^0)\) to \((\phi^1,q^1,r^1)\), cannot use (S1)-(S4) directly. We use a first-order backward-Euler (BE) self-starting step by default: a simpler, one-previous-level scheme whose local error is \(O(\Delta t^2)\), small enough that it does not degrade the second-order global rate of the rest of the trajectory (checked numerically, Section 7.2). A Richardson-extrapolated variant, built from two half-steps of BE, is also available for a formally second-order-accurate start.

## 4 The discrete energy identity

Discretising a dissipative system can destroy the property that makes it dissipative. A time- stepping scheme does not automatically inherit the energy decay of the continuous system it<tbc>

approximates. This is a real concern for our scheme: the freezing of the coefficients (Section 3) makes the equations linear, but it could have cost us the energy law. The discrete energy might then decrease only approximately, with an error that grows with \(\Delta t\), or it might decrease only for sufficiently small \(\Delta t\). The scheme (S1)-(S4) satisfies an exact discrete analogue of Proposition 2.1, with no approximation and no restriction on \(\Delta t\). Specifically, we construct a discrete energy E_n_ and a discrete dissipation \(\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}^{n+1}\), which have the same completed-square structure as the continuous dissipation D. They satisfy \(\mathcal{E}^{n+1}-\mathcal{E}^n=-\Delta t\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}^{n+1}-R^{n+1},\) where \(R^{n+1}\ge 0\) is an explicit non-negative remainder. This holds exactly, for every \(\Delta t>0\). We call a scheme unconditionally energy stable in this sense: the modified energy decreases at every step, by construction, for any step size, and not only once \(\Delta t\) is sufficiently small. Since BDF2 is a two-step method, the discrete energy E_n_ depends on two consecutive time levels, through the quadratic form \(\Phi\) (Section 3.1). The result relies on the coefficient freezing of Section 3. **Corollary 4.1** (Unconditional energy stability)**.** _Since every term after_ E<sup>_n_+1</sup>-E_<sup>n</sup> in_ (12) _is non-negative,_

\(\mathcal{E}^{n+1}\le\mathcal{E}^n\text{\textit{for every}}\Delta t>0.\)

_That is, the SAV-BDF2 scheme is unconditionally energy stable: the modified discrete energy never increases, at any step size. Since additionally_ \(\mathcal{E}^n\ge-C_0\) _is bounded below, the monotone sequence_ {E_<sup>n</sup>_} _converges._

**Remark 4.1** (The discrete energy bounds the solution)**.** Corollary 4.1 says that the modified energy E_<sup>n</sup>_ never increases. A decreasing energy is only useful if it also limits how large the fields can become. This is indeed the case.

The energy E_<sup>n</sup>_ is a sum of squares of \(\nabla\phi\), _q_ and _r_ at the two stored time levels _n_ and _n_-1. The two levels are combined through the form \(\Phi(u,v)=\|u\|^2+\|2u-v\|^2\). This combination is positive: it vanishes only if _u=v_=0, and it is bounded below and above by multiples of \(\|u\|^2+\|v\|^2\). Consequently, E_<sup>n</sup>+C_<sub>0</sub> is never smaller than a fixed positive multiple of

\(\gamma\left(\|\nabla\phi^n\|^2+\|\nabla\phi^{n-1}\|^2\right)+\|q^n\|^2+\|q^{n-1}\|^2+2\left((r^n)^2+(r^{n-1})^2\right).\)

Since \(\mathcal{E}^n\le\mathcal{E}^1\) for all \(n\ge 1\), none of these terms can exceed a fixed multiple of E<sup>1</sup>+_C_<sub>0</sub>. Hence \(\|\nabla\phi^n\|\), \(\|q^n\|\) and |_r<sup>n</sup>_| stay bounded for all times and for every \(\Delta t>0\).

Of the three quantities just bounded, _r_ already carries the effect of the bulk term \(E_f(\phi)\) by construction. What remains uncontrolled is \(\phi\) itself: E_<sup>n</sup>_ reaches \(\phi\) only through \(\nabla\phi\), and a gradient cannot see an additive constant, since \(\phi\) and \(\phi+\) const have the same gradient. The size of \(\phi\) itself is therefore controlled separately. By mass conservation (Proposition 5.1), the spatial average of \(\phi^n\) equals its initial value at every step. A field with fixed average and bounded gradient on a periodic domain cannot be arbitrarily large (Poincaré inequality), so \(\|\phi^n\|\) is bounded as well.

In summary, the numerical solution cannot blow up: \(\phi\), _q_ and _r_ remain bounded at all times, whatever the time step.

**Remark 4.2** (Stability of the filtered scheme actually used)**.** The long-time physics runs (Section 7.3) apply an optional 2/3-rule spectral filter _F_ to \((\phi,q)\) after every step (removing aliasing noise from evaluating nonlinear coefficients on the collocation grid). Since _F_ is an orthogonal, \(\nabla\)-commuting projection, a short argument (filtering cannot increase \(\Phi\): \(\Phi(Fu,v)=\Phi(u,v)-5\|(I-F)u\|^2\) for _Fv=v_; Appendix A) shows (12) extends exactly to the filtered scheme, with two explicit additional non-negative terms penalising the filtered-out content. Hence, the scheme actually producing the physics results shown in Section 7.3 is itself provably (not just empirically) stable for the same energy. We also confirmed numerically that both terms stay strictly positive, with genuine margin and not merely at round-off, over real trajectories.

**Remark 4.3** (Stability \(\neq\) accuracy)**.** Equation (12) does not show that \(\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}^{n+1}\), built from the extrapolated mobilities, approximates the physical dissipation D to second order under all circumstances. That is a consistency question settled, numerically in Section 7. Also, \(\mathcal{E}^n\neq E(\phi^n,q^n)\): the \(\Phi\)-form and (_r<sup>n</sup>_)<sup>2</sup>-_C_<sub>0</sub> each differ from the corresponding true quantities by \(O(\Delta t^2)\) (measured \(\approx 7\times 10^{-6}<\Delta t^2\)), so E_<sup>n</sup>_ decreases monotonically while \(E(\phi^n,q^n)\) may show \(O(\Delta t^2)\) non-monotonicities. Every figure claiming "energy decay" states which energy.

## 5 Structural properties

Section 4 showed that _if_ a solution of (S1)-(S4) exists at a given step, the discrete energy identity forces it to be well behaved: the modified energy can only decrease. That conditional phrasing hides a question energy stability alone does not answer: does (S1)-(S4), a linear system coupling four unknown fields at every step, actually _have_ a solution there, and is it unique? A scheme that<tbc>

<tbc>behaves well whenever it has a solution is of limited practical use if the underlying linear system can fail to be solvable, or have more than one solution, at some step sizes or some states; an implementation would then have no guarantee that the linear solve it calls every step is even well posed. This section closes that gap. Theorem 5.1 shows the linear system is uniquely solvable at _every_ step, for _every_ \(\Delta t>0\), reusing the energy identity of Theorem 4.1 itself as the proof’s main tool. Proposition 5.1 records a second structural property, exact mass conservation, needed along the way.

**Theorem 5.1** (Unconditional unique solvability)**.** _Under the same assumptions as Theorem 4.1, and additionally_ \(b_\star\ge b_1>0\)_, the linear system (S1)-(S4) is uniquely solvable for every_ \(\Delta t>0\).

_Proof._ Since (S1)-(S4) is linear, finite-dimensional, and square, existence and uniqueness for every choice of data are equivalent to the homogeneous system (all data set to zero) having only the trivial solution. So take a solution of (S1)-(S4) with \(\phi^n=\phi^{n-1}=q^n=q^{n-1}=r^n=r^{n-1}=0\). Plugging this data into (12) collapses it to a sum of non-negative terms equal to zero, which forces \(\nabla\phi^{n+1}=q^{n+1}=r^{n+1}=0\) and \(\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}^{n+1}=0\). Mass conservation (Proposition 5.1) then pins \(\phi^{n+1}\equiv 0\). With _q_<sup>_n_+1</sup>=0, the condition \(\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}^{n+1}=0\) reduces to \(\int_\Omega b_\star|\nabla\mu^{n+1}|^2=0\). Since \(b_\star\ge b_1>0\), this forces \(\nabla\mu^{n+1}=0\), so \(\mu^{n+1}\) is spatially constant, though not yet known to be zero. Equation (S2), with \(\phi^{n+1}\equiv 0\) and _r_<sup>_n_+1</sup>=0 already established, gives \(\mu^{n+1}=0\) directly, pinning that constant. So the homogeneous system has only the trivial solution, and (S1)-(S4) is uniquely solvable for every \(\Delta t>0\). Full proof in Appendix A.

**Proposition 5.1** (Exact mass conservation)**.** \(M^n:=\int_\Omega\phi^n\) _satisfies_ \(M^n\equiv M^0\) _for every n._

_Proof._ Test (S1) with the constant function 1. By (6a) with _g_=1, \(\left(\nabla\cdot F,1\right)=-\left(F,\nabla 1\right)=0\) for any flux _F_, since the gradient of a constant is zero; so the right-hand side of (S1) integrates to exactly zero, whatever \(\mu^{n+1},q^{n+1}\) turn out to be. The left-hand side, integrated, is \(\int_\Omega D_2\phi^{n+1}=\frac{1}{2\Delta t}\left(3M^{n+1}-4M^n+M^{n-1}\right)\) by the definition (7) of _D_<sub>2</sub>, so

\(3M^{n+1}-4M^n+M^{n-1}=0\) (14)

at every step \(n\ge 1\): a linear recursion relating three consecutive mass values, forced purely by the structure of (S1), regardless of \(\mu^{n+1},q^{n+1}\). The same argument, applied to the (simpler) backward- Euler startup step, gives _M_<sup>1</sup>=_M_<sup>0</sup>. We now show \(M^n\equiv M^0\) for every \(n\ge 0\) by induction: this holds for _n_=0,1 by definition and by the startup property just established. Suppose it holds up to some \(n\ge 1\), i.e. _M_<sup>_n_-1</sup>=_M<sup>n</sup>=M_<sup>0</sup>; then (14) gives 3_M_<sup>_n_+1</sup>=4_M<sup>n</sup>-M_<sup>_n_-1</sup>=4_M_<sup>0</sup>-_M_<sup>0</sup>=3_M_<sup>0</sup>, i.e. _M_<sup>_n_+1</sup>=_M_<sup>0</sup>, extending the claim to _n_+1. Hence \(M^n\equiv M^0\) for every _n_.

## 6 Accuracy and implementation

Theorems 4.1 and 5.1 establish that the scheme is unconditionally stable and solvable; neither says anything about whether it is actually _accurate_, or what turning (S1)-(S4) into working code involves. This section addresses both in turn. Algorithm 1 summarises the computation performed at every time step of the implementation used throughout the rest of the paper; the text below justifies why that computation is second-order accurate, and fills in the specific spatial discretisation and linear solver Algorithm 1 leaves unspecified.

### Accuracy.

The scheme’s formal order follows from a standard truncation argument, combining three separate sources of \(O(\Delta t^2)\) error into one. First, BDF2 itself contributes a local truncation error of \(O(\Delta t^2)\), by construction. Second, the extrapolation \(\phi^\star=\phi(t_{n+1})+O(\Delta t^2)\) (Section 3) makes every frozen coefficient consistent to the same order, _provided_ \(\phi^\star\) stays inside the clamp range; this proviso is verified to hold throughout the convergence regime studied below, so the clamp safeguard never actually bites and never degrades the order. Third, the SAV substitution<tbc>

<tbc>itself costs no further accuracy: \(r^{n+1}G_\star=f'(\phi^{n+1})+O(\Delta t^2)\), by the standard SAV consistency argument \[18\]. A local truncation error of \(O(\Delta t^3)\), accumulated over the \(O(1/\Delta t)\) steps of a fixed time horizon, gives a global error of \(O(\Delta t^2)\) overall; this is confirmed numerically in Section 7.2, including when the trajectory is started by the (only first-order-accurate) backward-Euler step of Algorithm 1. A rigorous relative-energy error estimate, in the style of \[6\], is left for future work.

## Spatial discretisation.

Space is discretised by periodic Fourier-Galerkin collocation on an \(N\times N\) grid, without 2/3-rule dealiasing by default (Remark 4.2 discusses the optional filter used for the long-time runs). This choice is exactly what Theorem 4.1 needs: exact discrete integration by parts and the commutation \(\nabla D_2=D_2\nabla\) both hold automatically for a periodic Fourier discretisation, with no further assumption, since every pointwise product entering the proof is formed directly on the collocation grid. One technical point is worth flagging explicitly, since it is easy to get wrong and silently breaks the identity if missed: the discrete Laplacian must use the symbol \(-(k_x^2\mathbf{1}_{k_x\neq N/2}+k_y^2\mathbf{1}_{k_y\neq N/2})\), zeroing out the Nyquist-frequency contribution in each direction, rather than the naive symbol -|_k_|<sup>2</sup>. With the naive symbol, the discrete gradient and Laplacian become subtly inconsistent at the Nyquist mode, and (12) fails outright once the solution develops any content at that frequency.

## Solving the linear system.

Step 4 of Algorithm 1, a (2_N_<sup>2</sup>+1)-dimensional linear system, is solved in one of two ways: by a dense direct solve, exact up to machine precision and so used as a ground-truth reference on small grids (\(N\lesssim 40\)); or by matrix-free GMRES (the generalised minimal residual method, an iterative solver for linear systems that does not require storing the system matrix) with a Fourier-diagonal preconditioner, built from the frozen coefficients reduced to representative scalars, used on the larger grids needed for the physics study. The two methods agree to 10<sup>-12</sup> wherever both are affordable. Throughout Section 7, an independent nonlinear reference solver is also used as a cross-check: it treats \(f'(\phi^{n+1})\) fully implicitly by Newton iteration, with no SAV device at all, on the identical spatial discretisation, so that any disagreement with the SAV scheme isolates exactly the effect of the SAV reformulation, and nothing else.

## Temporal and spatial convergence.

We check the scheme’s temporal order _p<sub>t</sub>_ (the exponent such that the error shrinks like \(\Delta t^{p_t}\)) in two independent ways. The first is the method of manufactured solutions (MMS) [25, 26], the standard technique for measuring a scheme’s convergence order when no closed-form solution of the original equations is available: we pick an arbitrary smooth function of (_x,t_), substitute it into (1), and add whatever extra forcing term is needed to make that function an exact solution of the resulting, slightly modified system (the explicit function and forcing term used here are given in Appendix B). Because the exact solution is then known in closed form, we can measure the true numerical error directly at each \(\Delta t\) and check how fast it shrinks as \(\Delta t\rightarrow 0\). Doing this with the reference configuration’s own \(b,c,A,\kappa\) forms, but with \(\gamma=0.30\) in place of 10<sup>-3</sup> and _N_=40 (both chosen large enough that the spatial grid is not the bottleneck at any \(\Delta t\) tested), gives _p<sub>t</sub>_≈2.00 for the backward-Euler startup and, for the Richardson startup, an order climbing from 1.68 to 1.95 as \(\Delta t\rightarrow 10^{-4}\), approaching 2 (Figure 4). The second check is directly at the physical \(\gamma=10^{-3}\) (_N_=160, tiny perturbation IC), where no manufactured solution is used; instead we estimate the order by self-convergence, comparing the numerical solutions obtained at successively halved \(\Delta t\) against one another rather than against a known exact solution, which gives _p<sub>t</sub>_=1.98,2.00. For the spatial discretisation, the Fourier-Galerkin method is expected to converge spectrally on smooth data, meaning the error should fall off faster than any fixed power of 1_/N_ as _N_ increases: starting from a smooth but sharply peaked (Lorentzian-shaped) initial condition and measuring the error relative to a highly resolved reference run at _N_=160, the error drops by a factor of 10<sup>7</sup> as _N_ increases from 16 to 96, confirming this spectral rate.

Two parameters entering the scheme are, by construction, not supposed to affect the computed solution, which we check here directly. ## Exact equivalence of the SAV reformulation.

The SAV trick replaces the nonlinear term \(f'(\phi)\) in (1b) by the product \(rG(\phi)\) of a new unknown _r(t_) and a known function _G_, and supplies _r_ with its own evolution equation. This is only useful if the enlarged system has exactly the same solutions as the original one. We show this by proving that, along any solution of the enlarged system, _r(t_) is forced to always equal \(\sqrt{E_f(\phi(t))+C_0}\), which is exactly the value that makes \(rG(\phi)\) equal \(f'(\phi)\).

With \(r(t):=\sqrt{E_f(\phi(t))+C_0}\) and \(G(\phi):=f'(\phi)/\sqrt{E_f(\phi)+C_0}\) (so, by construction, \(r(t)G(\phi(t))=f'(\phi(t))\) whenever _r(t_) happens to take this particular value), the SAV system replaces (1b) by \(\mu=-\gamma\Delta\phi+rG(\phi)\), where _r_ is now an independent unknown, and appends the equation \(\dot{r}=\frac{1}{2}\big(G(\phi)\), \(\partial_t\phi\big)\) to determine it. We must check that this new equation for _r_ is actually consistent with the formula that motivated it. By the chain rule,

\(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\sqrt{E_f(\phi(t))+C_0}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{E_f(\phi(t))+C_0}}\big(f'(\phi),\partial_t\phi\big).\)

If, at some instant, \(r=\sqrt{E_f(\phi)+C_0}\) already holds, then also \(f'(\phi)=rG(\phi)\) at that instant (by definition of _G_), so the right-hand side above becomes exactly \(\frac{1}{2}\big(G(\phi),\partial_t\phi\big)\), precisely the right-hand side of the SAV system’s own equation for \(\dot{r}\). In other words: the function \(t\mapsto\sqrt{E_f(\phi(t))+C_0}\) and any solution _r(t_) of the SAV system satisfy the same differential equation for \(\dot{r}\) (with \(\phi(t)\) regarded as already determined), and they start from the same value at _t_=0, since _r_(0) is initialised as \(\sqrt{E_f(\phi(0))+C_0}\).

Two functions of _t_ with the same derivative at every instant and the same value at one instant must be equal for all time: their difference has derivative zero everywhere and value zero at _t_=0, so by the fundamental theorem of calculus the difference is zero everywhere. Hence \(r(t)\equiv\sqrt{E_f(\phi(t))+C_0}\) along any solution of the SAV system, and therefore \(r(t)G(\phi(t))\equiv f'(\phi(t))\) for all _t_: the SAV \(\mu\)-equation reduces identically to the original (1b), so every solution of the SAV system solves (1). Conversely, given any solution of (1), defining \(r(t):=\sqrt{E_f(\phi(t))+C_0}\) satisfies the SAV system’s _r_-equation automatically, by the same chain-rule computation run in reverse: the two systems have exactly the same solutions.

Its role is to rewrite a term of the form \(\big(\)3_x_-4_y+z,x_\(\big)\), which arises whenever a BDF2 formula is tested against its newest level, as a telescoping difference of \(\Phi\) plus a non-negative remainder. This telescoping turns the step-by-step computation into a statement that the energy decreases monotonically. The identity is verified by expanding both sides into inner products and comparing coefficients. Let _x=a__n_+1, _y=an_, _z=a__n_-1, where _a_ denotes any of the quantities \(\nabla\phi\), _q_, _r_. ## Proof of the filtered-scheme stability extension (Remark 4.2).

When coefficients with strong curvature, such as _A<sub>⋆</sub>_ (which behaves like \(\mathrm{cot}(\pi\phi)\)), are evaluated pointwise on a spectral grid, products of fields can generate spurious high-frequency (aliasing) noise that has no counterpart in the continuous solution. For the long-time runs of Section 7.3, we suppress this noise by applying the 2/3-rule filter _F_ after every step. The filter discards the highest third of the resolved wavenumbers in each direction.

Filtering changes the fields that are stored and used in the next step. Therefore, Theorem 4.1, which was proved for the unfiltered scheme, does not apply directly to the scheme that is actually run. We show here that the identity (12) extends to the filtered scheme, with two additional non-negative terms. Consequently, the scheme that produced the results of Section 7.3 is provably stable.

### Properties of the filter.

In Fourier space, _F_ multiplies each mode by 1 (kept) or 0 (discarded), depending only on the wavenumber. Hence _F_ is diagonal in the Fourier basis, which gives three properties:

• _F_<sup>2</sup>=_F_, since multiplying a mode by 0 or 1 twice is the same as doing so once;<tbc>

• _F_<sup>∗</sup>=_F_, since _F_ is a real diagonal operator in an orthonormal basis;<tbc>

• \(\nabla F=F\nabla\), since \(\nabla\) is also diagonal in the Fourier basis, and diagonal operators commute.

It follows that _F(I-F_)=_F-F_<sup>2</sup>=0, and therefore \(\big(\)_Fu,_ (_I-F)u_\(\big)=\(\big(\)_u, F(I-F)u_\(\big)\)=0 for every field _u_. In particular,<tbc>

\(\|u\|^2=\|Fu\|^2+\|(I-F)u\|^2.\) (26)

<tbc>_Effect of the filter on_ \(\Phi\). Let _v_ be a field with _Fv=v_, and let _u_ be arbitrary. We claim that<tbc>

\(\Phi(u,v)-\Phi(Fu,v)=5\|(I-F)u\|^2.\) (27)

<tbc>The first term of \(\Phi\) is handled by (26): \(\|u\|^2-\|Fu\|^2=\|(I-F)u\|^2\). For the second term, write 2_u-v_=(2_Fu-v_)+2(_I-F)u_. Since _Fv=v_, the field 2_Fu-v_ lies in the range of _F_ and is therefore orthogonal to (_I-F)u_. Hence

\(\|2u-v\|^2=\|2Fu-v\|^2+4\|(I-F)u\|^2.\)

Adding the two differences gives \(\|(I-F)u\|^2+4\|(I-F)u\|^2=5\|(I-F)u\|^2\), which proves (27). Thus, filtering can only decrease \(\Phi\), and the decrease is exactly five times the squared norm of the removed part.

### Application to the scheme.

At each step, the stored previous levels are outputs of the filter, so the hypothesis _Fv=v_ holds for them (by induction over the steps, with filtered initial data). We apply (27) with

• \(u=\nabla\phi^{n+1}\) and \(v=\nabla\phi^n\), where \(\phi^n\) is the stored, already filtered field (note that \(\nabla F=F\nabla\));<tbc>

• _u=q_<sup>_n_+1</sup> and _v=q<sup>n</sup>_;<tbc>

• _u=r_<sup>_n_+1</sup> and _v=r<sup>n</sup>_. Here no filtering is applied to the scalar _r_, so this pair contributes nothing.

Replacing the raw fields \(\phi^{n+1},q^{n+1}\) by their filtered versions \(F\phi^{n+1},Fq^{n+1}\) in E<sup>_n_+1</sup> lowers it by

\(\frac{5\gamma}{4}\|(I-F)\nabla\phi^{n+1}\|^2+\frac{5}{4}\|(I-F)q^{n+1}\|^2\ge 0.\)

Therefore (12) holds for the filtered scheme with these two non-negative terms added on the dissipative side. In particular, Corollary 4.1 remains valid: the modified energy of the stored (filtered) fields does not increase, for every \(\Delta t>0\).

For zero previous-level data, E_n_=-_C_0, and, using \(\Phi(u,0)=5\|u\|^2\), \(\mathcal{E}^{n+1}+C_0=\frac{5}{4}\big[\gamma\|\nabla\psi\|^2+\|\chi\|^2+2\rho^2\big].\) The identity (12) holds for arbitrary previous-level data, so it holds here as well. Inserting the expressions above (the remainder term in (12) contributes \(\frac{1}{4}[\gamma\|\nabla\psi\|^2+\|\chi\|^2+2\rho^2]\)) gives \(\frac{3}{2}\big[\gamma\|\nabla\psi\|^2+\|\chi\|^2+2\rho^2\big]+\Delta t\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}=0,\) where \(\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}\) is (11) evaluated at \((\nu,\chi)\). Since \(\gamma>0\), and \(\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}\ge 0\) by Assumption 1 (as in Step 5 of the proof of Theorem 4.1), all terms are non-negative. Hence each of them vanishes: \(\nabla\psi=0,\chi=0,\rho=0,\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}=0.\) ### Step 2: \(\psi=0\). Since \(\nabla\psi=0\), the function \(\psi\) is constant in space. To determine the constant, we test (S1) with 1. By (6a) with _g_=1, the right-hand side integrates to zero, so \(\int_\Omega D_2\psi=\frac{3}{2\Delta t}\int_\Omega\psi=0\). Thus \(\psi\) has zero mean. A constant function with zero mean on \(\Omega\) vanishes, so \(\psi=0\). _Step 3:_ \(\nu=0\). With \(\chi=0\), the integrand of \(\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}\) simplifies, because \(\big(b_\star-\frac{c_\star^2}{d_0}\big)+\frac{c_\star^2}{d_0}=b_\star\): \(\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}=\int_\Omega\big(b_\star-\frac{c_\star^2}{d_0}\big)|\nabla\nu|^2+\frac{1}{d_0}\int_\Omega|c_\star\nabla\nu|^2=\int_\Omega b_\star|\nabla\nu|^2.\) Since \(\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}=0\) and \(b_\star\ge b_1>0\), we obtain \(\nabla\nu=0\), so \(\nu\) is constant in space. (This is the only place where the additional assumption \(b_\star\ge b_1>0\) is used.) The constant is fixed by (S2): with \(\psi=0\) and \(\rho=0\), it reads \(\nu=-\gamma\Delta\psi+\rho G_\star=0\). We have shown \(\psi=\nu=\chi=\rho=0\). Thus the homogeneous system has only the trivial solution, and (S1)-(S4) has a unique solution for every \(\Delta t>0\) and for arbitrary data \((\phi^n,q^n,r^n)\) and \((\phi^{n-1},q^{n-1},r^{n-1})\). ## B The manufactured solution used in Section 7.2 The temporal MMS check of Section 7.2 uses the explicit, smooth functions \(\phi_\mathrm{ex}(x,y,t):=0.5+0.15\mathrm{cos}(2\pi x)\mathrm{cos}(2\pi y)e^{-3t},q_\mathrm{ex}(x,y,t):=0.10\mathrm{sin}(2\pi x)\mathrm{sin}(2\pi y)e^{-2t},\) on \(\Omega=(0,1)^2\) at \(\gamma=0.30\), chosen large enough that \(\phi=0.5\) is not spimodally unstable for this low wavenumber, so the forced problem below is not numerically stiff. Neither function solves (1). With \(\mu_\mathrm{ex}:=-\gamma\Delta\phi_\mathrm{ex}+f'(\phi_\mathrm{ex})\), define the forcing pair \(S_\phi(t):=\partial_t\phi_\mathrm{ex}(t)-\nabla\cdot\big(b(\phi_\mathrm{ex})\nabla\mu_\mathrm{ex}-c(\phi_\mathrm{ex})\nabla(A(\phi_\mathrm{ex})q_\mathrm{ex})\big),\)
\(S_q(t):=\partial_tq_\mathrm{ex}(t)-\big[-\kappa(\phi_\mathrm{ex})q_\mathrm{ex}-A(\phi_\mathrm{ex})\nabla\cdot\big(c(\phi_\mathrm{ex})\nabla\mu_\mathrm{ex}-d_0\nabla(A(\phi_\mathrm{ex})q_\mathrm{ex})\big)+\varepsilon_q\Delta q_\mathrm{ex}\big],\)

where \(\partial_t\phi_\mathrm{ex},\partial_tq_\mathrm{ex}\) are the known, closed-form time derivatives of the two functions above. By construction, \(S_\phi,S_q\) are exactly the residuals of (1a),(1c) at \((\phi_\mathrm{ex},q_\mathrm{ex})\). Adding \(S_\phi,S_q\) to the right-hand sides of (1a),(1c) makes \((\phi_\mathrm{ex},q_\mathrm{ex})\) an exact solution of the resulting, forced system. At the discrete level, \(S_\phi,S_q\) are evaluated at _t_<sub>_n_+1</sub> (using the same discrete spatial operators as the scheme itself) and added to the right-hand sides of (S1),(S3) only; (S4) is left untouched, since its correctness follows once \(\phi^{n+1}\) already matches \(\phi_\mathrm{ex}\). The resulting forced scheme has a known exact solution at every \(\Delta t\), so the error \(\|\phi^n-\phi_\mathrm{ex}(t_n)\|_\infty\) can be measured directly. Because \((\phi_\mathrm{ex},q_\mathrm{ex})\) does not solve the unforced system, this forced run is not expected to, and does not, satisfy the energy identity (12). The check is purely about the truncation-error order, not about stability.
